Motor racing-Formula E reschedules Saudi Arabian season opener due to conflict Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 17:30 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 17:30 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The all-electric Formula E series announced the rescheduling of its Saudi Arabian season-opener on Thursday due to conflict in the region, with the championship now due to start in Mexico City in January. The double-header in Jeddah was originally scheduled for December 18-19 but is now pencilled in for April 16 and 17 as the season's sixth and seventh races. The Mexico City round will kick off the campaign on January 16. "I guess the news which may not come as a surprise to anybody is that we are looking to change the order of the racing calendar," Formula E chief executive Jeff Dodds told reporters in a video call citing "the conflict ongoing in the Middle East" and the logistical impact. "We will no longer start the season in Jeddah in December as planned," he said. "We will schedule Jeddah in for the Friday and Saturday of 16th, 17th of April. And in order to accommodate that change we will move the Sanya race (in China) to the 3rd of April, two weeks forward." That change also avoids a clash with the Chinese Formula One Grand Prix being held in Shanghai on April 18 and compresses the calendar from a 2026-27 one to a championship held within the space of seven months in 2027. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) is a principal partner of Formula E and also has a 5% stake in the FIA-sanctioned series. A number of sporting events in Saudi Arabia have been cancelled or postponed, including the final round of the World Rally Championship in November and January's Dakar Rally, as a result of attacks by Yemen's Houthis on Saudi Arabia, including on civilian airports and critical infrastructure. Dodds said keeping the Saudi races on the calendar had been his main focus and there was no conversation ongoing with any other circuit about eventually replacing them should April also prove impossible. "I would say that if the race can't go ahead in April, we would look at potentially other options to schedule the race (in 2027)," he explained, saying a decision would have to be made by mid- to late February. "But I think candidly at this stage what we wouldn't look to do is replace Jeddah with another location. "I think what's much more likely is that if Jeddah can't go ahead in April we end up with a reduced schedule." Dodds said the postponement had been a "fully collegiate" decision with agreement from PIF and the governing FIA. "They want this race to go ahead and to go ahead well and the best way of currently delivering that is to move it back in the schedule to allow things more time to settle," he added. Formula E is due to start testing its new Gen4 car at Spain's Jarama circuit next week.

American Cancer Society calls for routine prostate cancer screening in guideline change Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 17:30 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 17:30 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Routine prostate cancer screening is now advised for many men, the American Cancer Society announced on Thursday in a major guideline change, saying it believes the possible benefits now outweigh potential harms given medical advances and accumulating evidence. Its previous guideline issued in 2010 advised men to decide whether to undergo screening after discussing possible advantages and disadvantages with healthcare providers. “Back in 2010, we actually didn't have a strong opinion on whether or not one should be screened,” said ACS Chief Scientific Officer Dr. William Dahut in an interview. “It was unclear at that point whether the potential harms outweighed the benefits.” An estimated 333,830 US men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2026 and an estimated 36,320 men will die of the disease, the ACS said. The updated guideline recommends blood tests to measure prostate-specific antigen levels every two years for average-risk men ages 50 to 69, and annual screening for men with a family history of prostate cancer. For Black men, who have a 67% higher incidence and nearly double the mortality rate compared with white men, it now recommends annual prostate cancer screening for ages 45 to 69. “By making a direct recommendation for men to engage in screening and advocating for earlier and more frequent screening for Black men, our aim is also to help reduce prostate cancer disparities and ease the disease burden,” Dahut said. The balance of benefits and harms remains uncertain for men ages 70 to 74, who should discuss screening with their doctors, according to the guideline. Screening is not recommended for men 75 and older, although some men ages 75 to 79 who are very healthy may want to continue screening, especially if their PSA level has been rising on previous tests, the ACS says. Screening is not recommended for men 80 and older or for men who are not expected to live another 10 years. The possible benefits and harms of universal prostate cancer screening have been hotly debated for years. The fear was that it would identify too many cancers that would never have produced symptoms, in which case treatment could cause side effects such as incontinence and impotence without significant benefits. The changes, detailed in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, reflect stronger evidence of the benefits of PSA-based screening combined with the increasing use of management strategies that can reduce harms, such as unnecessary biopsies and treatment side effects, the ACS said. The new guidelines – which still say men should receive information about the risks and benefits before PSA testing – now call for a repeat blood test and a magnetic resonance imaging study before a biopsy is scheduled. Men diagnosed with low-risk prostate cancer should initially be offered close monitoring rather than active treatment, the guideline says. Doctors have gotten much better at distinguishing men who have high-risk prostate cancer from those who can safely delay treatment, Dahut said. Treatments now have fewer side effects, robotic surgery has raised the quality of care, and radiation treatments are more targeted and of higher quality, he added.

item.content:encoded:
US envoys go to Kremlin for talks with Putin on Ukraine   Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 17:29 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 17:29 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived at the Kremlin on Thursday for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, in a new push for a peace deal in Ukraine despite what they have called a lack of trust between Moscow and Kyiv. The negotiations are the 10th time Witkoff has met Putin in person during a conflict that has lasted longer than the Soviet Union's fight against Nazi Germany in World War Two, and follow two days of US-led trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi. After the Abu Dhabi talks, the first direct US-mediated negotiations between Russia and Ukraine in nine months, the sides said they had agreed on a major exchange of prisoners of war that is likely to happen in the coming weeks, but announced no breakthrough in wider negotiations. As he entered a Moscow hotel before the Kremlin talks, Witkoff was asked by a reporter whether progress made in the talks so far meant peace was closer. "I hope so," he replied. Russian and Ukrainian negotiators reported some progress in Abu Dhabi, but the US side said differences remained on major issues, including territory. Witkoff and Kushner are expected to fly to Dublin later on Thursday for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who said on Wednesday he hoped a result in the talks could be achieved by the end of this year, but that much depended on how the United States approached Moscow. President Donald Trump, who once said he could end the now 4-1/2-year-old conflict in 24 hours, has instructed Witkoff and Kushner, his son-in-law, to make a new push for peace, which he hopes will burnish his self-styled credentials as a peacemaker. He said last week that the conflict was close to being settled in a "big beautiful agreement", though he has frequently predicted breakthroughs that have not materialised. DISAGREEMENT ON TERRITORY Kyiv has rejected a demand by Putin, who sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022, to surrender the whole of the eastern Donbas region in return for peace - something Russian forces are trying to achieve on the battlefield in the face of fierce Ukrainian resistance. Moscow has not made major territorial gains this year, but has heavily attacked Ukrainian infrastructure and Kyiv has frequently struck Russian oil refineries with drones, causing fuel shortages over the summer, a problem which has resurfaced in some regions this week according to local officials. Putin has shown no signs of being ready to moderate his territorial demands, which include a buffer zone in parts of Ukraine which Russia has not formally claimed as its own. Vladimir Medinsky, Putin's lead negotiator in the Abu Dhabi talks, told state TV on Wednesday that "wherever the foot of our Russian soldier has stepped, that is ours." He was also cited by the TASS state news agency as saying that "every inch" of what Moscow regards as Russian land would be returned. There is tension too over a Ukrainian and European desire - backed by the United States - for the European Union, whose big member states are staunch backers of Kyiv, to have a seat at the negotiating table. The Kremlin has said that the EU should be included in the talks at some stagebut has poured cold water on the idea in recent days. It points to a lack of constructive proposals from Brussels and an inability by the EU to select someone to represent it in any future talks, and says it lacks realism. Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief, accused Russia on Monday of pretending to negotiate and said Moscow had shown no goodwill in talks while continuing to bomb Kyiv. With talks deadlocked on territory, US mediators have tried to steer discussions towards post-war security guarantees and reconstruction, and Russia has spoken of the need to agree on a post-war security framework for Europe. A senior Russian diplomat said on Wednesday that Moscow could conclude non-aggression pacts with NATO member states. But the idea of discussing such matters has stirred fears in Kyiv and among its allies too. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday that wider European security talks should come only once there is a ceasefire in Ukraine. Moscow has rejected the idea of a temporary ceasefire, saying it wants an overall deal to end the war rather than a pause in which Ukraine might re-arm. (Reporting by Reuters, Writing by Andrew Osborn, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

China's premier calls for broader, fairer and more sustainable social security coverage Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 17:20 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 17:20 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

China's Premier Li Qiang called for improvements in the country's social security system to make it fair and sustainable while broadening its coverage, state media reported on Thursday, citing a study session of the country's cabinet. Changes in demographics, technology and new forms of employment have created new demands on social security, Li said, stressing the need to "fully recognize the important role social security plays in overall development." China should improve social security coverage for workers in non-traditional, flexible employment, and gradually improve their social insurance coverage, Li said. It should also move faster to close gaps in the social security system, broaden access to employer-sponsored retirement plans, and make voluntary personal pension schemes more appealing to the public, he said.
